blocks.content: kubectl create is the imperative counterpart to apply, a one-time creation command, useful for quick, direct object creation, without necessarily needing a YAML file at all.
create does exactly one thing: creates a new object, right now, it has no concept of "update if it already exists," that is precisely the gap apply, covered in the previous topic, fills.

blocks.alt: A single, direct action, nothing more nuanced than that

blocks.content: 2. Creating Directly, Without a YAML File
blocks.text: 2. Creating Directly, Without a YAML File

blocks.content: Unlike apply, create can build simple objects directly from command-line flags, no manifest file needed at all, genuinely convenient for a quick, one-off object.

blocks.alt: A quick, direct shortcut, no manifest file required

blocks.content: 3. Fails if the Object Already Exists
blocks.text: 3. Fails if the Object Already Exists

blocks.content: This is the genuinely important limitation, running create against an object that already exists simply fails with an error, it makes no attempt to reconcile or update anything.

blocks.alt: A hard failure, not a graceful update, if the object is already there

blocks.content: 4. When to Reach for This vs apply
blocks.text: 4. When to Reach for This vs apply

blocks.content: create genuinely fits quick, one-off experiments and imperative scripting, apply fits real, ongoing, repeatable workflows, most production usage, and most of this course's examples, favor apply for exactly that reason.

blocks.alt: A quick, imperative shortcut versus the repeatable, declarative standard

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: kubectl create is a one-time, imperative creation command, it can build simple objects directly from flags, without a YAML file, but fails if the object already exists.
Real, ongoing workflows favor apply for exactly this reason, its ability to safely handle both "create" and "update" cases without failing.
